utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is the case number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin and Momir Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's go through the usual routine. First, 30 seconds or a minute wasted of the morning. Mr. Brdjanin, good morning to you. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Yes, I can hear you and understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. General Talic, good morning to you. Are you hearing me in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED TALIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours, I can hear you and I can understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: While you are -- you may sit down, but I would like to know from you, again, confirmation that you have no objection to this sitting to go on, considering that none of the two counsel assigned to you are present.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED TALIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no objection and I agree that we continue with the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, General Talic. Appearances for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Nicholas Koumjian and Joanna Korner for the Prosecution, and excuse me, also Nicola Hamilton, case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I was going to run out and make an appointment with my eye specialist. It reminds me, I had a friend of mine, a judge actually, who fell doing some work on a matter and he tripped, fell, hit his head and for some time he was seeing double. And when the Chief Justice and myself went to see him and he told us that he was seeing double, Chief Justice said, "That's the best piece of news I've heard for some time, because at the end of the month, I will send you half a paycheque." Appearances for Mr. Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: John Ackerman and Tania Radosavljevic, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Appearances for General Talic. Don't tell me that Maitre de Roux and Maitre Pitron are here because I will get furious.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President and Your Honours. I was just waiting for the interpretation. I'm Natasha Fauveau-Ivanovic and I'm assisted by Mr. Fabien Masson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you and I hope that, as you promised, by Monday this situation will be cleared for the benefit of you all. And also for the tranquility of the mind of this Trial Chamber. The understanding for today is that we will continue, of course, with the cross-examination of Mr. Krzic and then with whatever follows, or after that, and then we will deal with a few issues that we have not necessarily pending but which we think that -- ought to be discussed before we continue, particularly items that were raised during the meeting that you had with Mr. Von Hebel and also additional matters that have emerged in the course of this week. So thank you. Could you please bring in the witness? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Krzic, it's barely necessary for me to remind you that you will be continuing giving testimony on the same solemn declaration that you made yesterday and on previous occasions, that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I have tried to reduce a great deal some of the things I wanted to ask Mr. Krzic in an effort to try to finish within a couple of hours, as I told you I would try to do yesterday. We will just have to see how it goes. I'll do my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Krzic, good morning.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What I'm going to try to do today, Mr. Krzic, at least with many of my questions, is to frame them in a way that you can answer them with either a yes or a no, because we have a lot of material to get through and I'd like to get through it if we can today. Understand that if you somehow feel a need to explain your answer beyond a yes or no, I'm certain that the Trial Chamber will permit you to do that. But let's, please, do the best we can to move through this material. I will tell you that if you are not answering the question that I ask you, if you don't understand it, you can ask me to repeat it. If you are not answering, please, understand that I will stop you and ask you to please answer the question that I've asked you. And that way, we can get this finished. Does that sound okay to you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. We were talking yesterday about the arming of Muslim people in the Banja Luka area and the last question that I had asked you was with regard to the Vecici fighters and whether or not they were getting weapons from this person Salih and you had told me that they were. My next question is: They were also getting weapons from a Serb soldier who had stolen weapons from storage, were they not?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not able to answer that question because I don't know for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The witness needs to have his statements with him again, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm on page 26 of the third statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of the third statement. The third statement, just to make sure that we are in agreement, is the one which is based on the interviews that took place between the 10th and 14th of December, 10th, 12th, 14th and 15th of February, 2001, no?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Yes, Mr. -- please, page?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Twenty-six, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Have you found that page, Mr. Krzic, page 26?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The paragraph I'm referring to begins -- it's near the bottom of the page, starts with the language, "On page 133." And it says, "You had gotten some information from a Bosniak in Banja Luka about Serb soldiers stealing weapons from a known underground military storage and selling them to the Vecici fighters. That's what you said, correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember saying that in relation to Vecici, but I said that I did have information that someone did provide rifles from storage. I didn't say that in relation to Vecici. I do not have any such knowledge, nor did I ever have any such knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Have you read that paragraph that begins with, "On page 133," begins with that language, at page 26 of that statement?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the Bosnian version in front of me. I said that I -- in Vecici, in order to gain their trust, I said that they had obtained weapons in Banja Luka and from whom. But it doesn't say from a Serb, nor how many weapons. It could have been a pistol or a rifle but certainly not heavy weapons, because that would be absurd. So I don't see how it is possible that in the English version mention is made of a Serb providing weapons for the fighters of Vecici. I never mentioned that. And I think that it was in the translation that an error was made.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Would you please read the rest of that paragraph? You read the first sentence. Read the rest of it, please. You can read either version you want, either the B/C/S or the English. I don't care.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I had heard but I didn't say that to the people of Vecici. I told them that I knew where they may have obtained weapons from but I didn't link it to this statement of this Serb. These are two quite separate things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think he has answered your question more than once already, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Would you look at statement number 1, please? Find statement number 1 for me. It's over here in this stack.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Number 1?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I want to direct you to page 22?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Would you please go and help witness with the document? This is the statement which is based on the interviews held on -- in 1994, 1995 -- 1994, 1995, in December, March, April, May and August of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Should be marked number 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Page, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Twenty-two.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Here there are not enough pages, there are more than 30.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Have you found page 22?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: This part of your statement refers to a meeting that you had with General Talic prior to the events that occurred in Kozarac and Prijedor. In the large paragraph, about two-thirds of the way down the page, there is language as follows: "General Talic could not afford a rebellion in Banja Luka for three reasons: A, it would tie up some of his forces and upset the supply of provisions to the front; B, he knew that there would be a large number of victims; and C, the political consequence internationally would be grave. Banja Luka had already become a focus of international attention thanks to the activities of the SDA. Several months prior to this meeting, we held several meetings with American senators. General Talic was also aware of the fact that the Bosnians had several thousand weapons in their possession. He was also aware of the fact that if a rebellion took place, then we would be joined by Croats and the number of victims would be very great." My only question is: Did you say that and is it true?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is my position, that is my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Before I move to the next area, you had mentioned in your direct examination that you knew the licence tag number of a red kombi that you were talking about in Banja Luka. Could you tell us that licence tag number, please?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I knew it, but the people who were victims of soldiers from that van, on one occasion, noted down that number and I can find it in the book. I can't memorise it. If necessary, I can find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let me ask you to do that when we take the break and be prepared to tell me that number when we come back. Will you do that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But Mr. Ackerman, in view of the warning that you gave me, it is quite possible that there may have been several such red vans. I don't think that there was just one for the whole of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You had -- the only one I'm talking about is you told us on direct examination that you knew the licence tag number of a red kombi and I'm only asking you to give us that tag number that you mentioned on direct, if you can find it. If you can't, I'll understand. This incident about the Vecici fighters, can you tell us approximately when it was that you were asked to become involved in efforts to get them to surrender? When in time?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember the exact date now, but it has been repeated so many times. What I can say is that it was immediately after a meeting with Mr. Peter Galbraith and members of his staff. When I was invited to the municipal assembly, the president of the HDZ came, and I was invited to a talk with Mr. Kupresanin in the municipal assembly about Vecici. I was in company. With me was Mr. Alan Novan (phoen). So if we can find that date, and in any event, it was the summer of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good enough, summer of 1992 is good enough. The person trying to get you to become involved and arrange for the surrender was Vojo Kupresanin, correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And at that time, he was president of the ARK Assembly, Autonomous Region of Krajina Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And in that process, he had threatened to personally put you in Manjaca if you didn't show up and go to Vecici to arrange for the surrender, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not right. He threatened only after the negotiations failed. He requested that I go again and it was then that he threatened, when he demanded that I go again.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There was a time when he threatened to put you in Manjaca, right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I was saying, only after the first negotiations failed and when he asked me to go and negotiate surrender again, then he threatened personally to take me to Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that concerned you a great deal, that you were threatened with that, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. For me, I consider that my life was at risk.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you contacted and explained this to Mr. Kelly, did you not?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By telephone, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And Mr. Kelly was with the American embassy in Belgrade, correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And then you got a telephone call from someone at the Jewish Federation in New York telling you that he would call General Talic and Mr. Panic in Belgrade with regard to the matter. That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that he said that he would talk to Mr. Panic, and he asked who was the most responsible person in Banja Luka at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And so you gave him Mr. Kupresanin's name? Or whose name did you give him when he asked who the most responsible person was?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I gave him the name of General Talic and the name of the municipality president, Mr. Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, Predrag Radic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: With regard to Predrag Radic, in your statement you mention a time that you had been in a meeting with Predrag Radic, and at the close of the meeting apparently he pulled you aside and said to you, "Stojan Zupljanin was responsible for everything that was happening in Banja Luka." Do you remember that incident?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And what you said in your statement was that you kept this information quiet in the hopes that Mr. Radic would give you additional valuable information in the future, correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't publicise that, certainly, for several reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, there are some documents that I want Mr. Krzic to be able to refer to, if he wishes. I had advised the Prosecutor yesterday of which ones I was going to be referring to and I think they were pulling them for us so he could be supplied with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: These are the ones that were distributed yesterday? This pile?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No. This is just a small number of documents that Mr. Krzic had attached, had supplied with regard to his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, we need to know what documents are we talking about now. I mean it's -- because it's not clear. Yesterday I found this pile on my desk.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We will be coming to that. Those are Defence exhibits that I'll be using.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I imagine so. So what are you going to ask him questions about? Which documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: These are documents that were supplied by the Prosecution, that he supplied the Prosecution in connection with his efforts to help the Prosecution understand his testimony, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, do you know which documents Mr. Ackerman is referring to?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. He gave us a list of documents that he was going to refer to yesterday. I'm afraid, however, there has been a slight misunderstanding. As the Defence wanted to put them to him, we thought the Defence were going to supply copies, so we haven't actually pulled them, as Mr. Ackerman suggests. I don't think it would be very difficult to find them but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are we in possession of them? In other words, all the documents that were exhibited or admitted in the course of Mr. Krzic's evidence, I have in this folder here. Are we talking of documents that I ought to find in this folder or are they new documents --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- that we haven't seen before.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I rather think they were -- I personally am afraid I have not gone through them, but I rather think they are not documents that you're going to find in the Banja Luka binders. But I need to do a Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. double-check. I'm afraid that we have all been working on the basis that if the Defence were going to put the documents, they were going to supply, but I'd need to do a double-check. At any rate, at the moment all I can say is we were given a pile of documents yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I rather thought that's what Mr. Ackerman was going to put to the witness this morning. I'm obviously wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, there is obviously --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have these documents handy?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I have them and I will not go to them now, I'll wait until after the break. I'll get copies done during the break and be ready to use them. There was clearly a misunderstanding between me and the Prosecutor yesterday. We will get it straightened out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Krzic, where I want to go now is to the book, "Life and Death Under Occupation." I don't know what you have before you, whether you have that book before you or not and whether you have the English translations that have been provided of pages from that book, but if you do not, I'd ask that it be supplied to you so we can refer to it.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the book in Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The difficulty I suppose --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which -- can I, again, interrupt for a moment and add some information as to which book you're referring to, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Called "Life and Death Under Occupation," January 4th, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Who wrote this book?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Krzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: That's incorrect --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The translation from Mr. Krzic's -- part of Mr. Krzic's book that we have is a partial English translation of crimes against the Banja Luka Krajina, 1992, 1994, Muharem Krzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's the other book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is the only translation that we have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Perhaps I could assist. What Mr. Ackerman is calling a book, I imagine, was published as a book, but this was not written by Mr. Krzic. What this is, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I remember Mr. Krzic answering one of the very first questions, is this the only book that you wrote, and he said yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: This material, "Life and Death Under Occupation," was apparently published by the Bosnian mission to the United Nations. It says at the top, "Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina Permanent Mission to the United Nations." It's a collection of documents that were faxed generally through Mr. Krzic, either authored by him or he forwarded them on to the embassy, so he is the author of many of the documents in this material. But it was published, to my knowledge, only in English. We may have translated it into B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But if it was published in New York, probably by Muhamed Sacirbey, I can assure you it would be very strange if it was published in Serbo-Croat. Because this was for dissemination in New York so what I would -- but we don't have a copy of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We will probably have to deal with that during the break too, then, Your Honour, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I can make a copy of it. I have one with me. I can either give it to the witness now or I can copy it for the Court and council. Some of the documents that were used during his direct came from that material.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please, if we can go ahead and do that, we can do it. Because the break, we still have another hour before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I have plenty of things to do, Your Honour. No shortage of material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm going now to some things that you talked about in your direct testimony. When did your wife leave Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My wife left at the end of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Had she been employed in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Odzicajvic factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And what was her position in that factory?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She was head of one of the laboratories. She is a technology engineer of chemical technology.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And was she dismissed from her job?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When was she dismissed from her job?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that period of widespread dismissals.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Dismissed by whom?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the authorities in the administration of Odzicajvic, but even if she hadn't been dismissed, she wouldn't have dared go to work because there were constant threats.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Which is it? Did she stop going to work or was she actually dismissed?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She was dismissed, like the other non-Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Why did she leave Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She left because the danger for families was growing. She is a woman and she could have easily been arrested and raped.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And where did she go?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She went to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You said that she went in the last convoy to leave Banja Luka; is that true?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I can't remember that particular moment because, for me, that was tragic and it's very difficult for me to recollect without prior warning so that I can look it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, there weren't any convoys leaving Banja Luka, ever, were there?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Will you, please, tell me where you found that? I will look it up and give you a precise answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm just asking you the question. There weren't ever any convoys leaving Banja Luka, were there?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Will you, please -- if you're asking me about my son's departure, I can remember exactly because I saw him off myself. As far as my wife is concerned, just now, I can't remember. Maybe because she died in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm not asking you, sir, about your wife or your son, and I'm sorry about even raising this issue with you, but my question is simple. There weren't ever any convoys that left Banja Luka, were there?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course there were. There were for a time, then they were prohibited, then they were resumed. Of course there were. In May, there was even an air link. The last planes went in May, just before the attack on Kozarac. I think it was my son that left on one of those planes and via Belgrade, he moved to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Those planes were going to Belgrade, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We talked a bit yesterday, and I want to talk a little bit more, about the two votes that were held. There were both a plebiscite and a referendum, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the referendum took place because the Badinter Commission had ordered that there be a referendum in Bosnia-Herzegovina because it appeared that the Serb population was opposed to independence and they wanted a referendum to see what the will of the population was?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the Serbian plebiscite was asking Serbs if they wanted to remain in Yugoslavia, correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but that happened at sometime earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, it did. And the referendum which was boycotted by the Serbs was asking voters if they were in favour of independence?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's more or less correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. You told us when you were talking about the things that were happening in Banja Luka between April and December of 1992 that many people had to change their names and be re-christened in order to keep their jobs. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Can you give us the name of one person who was forced to change their name?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can but I don't see why I should do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, just -- I'd just like to know the name of one person that --

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... change their name?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I might expose such a person to danger, at his workplace.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Would you be willing to give us the name if we were in closed session so that nobody could hear you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Can we just do that quickly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What is the relevance of the question? Why do you want to extract from the witness any particular name?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: To be able to investigate that and determine if he's telling us the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then I obviously agree with him that he shouldn't be made to mention any name at random. Why should one person be selected simply because Mr. Krzic chooses at any given moment to mention that particular person and not another so that you can investigate?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I think I should be able to investigate the veracity of his testimony to Your Honours and I can't do that if he won't give me the name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The rest of his testimony, I think, finishes here in the sense that he has told you that if we are in closed session he's prepared to give you a name. But I'm not prepared to allow him to give us names, not in this fashion. I mean if there is any particular person that you have in mind and that you would like to have conduct investigations upon, yes, but not at random. I mean you just ask him. He may have his own reasons why he should mention one person rather than another.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the next thing is that he could give us a name and frankly, I don't know how you can proceed with investigating further unless then he gives us a hell of a lot more information about this particular person. And I don't think we should be moving in that direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: For the record, Your Honour, I urge that I be permitted to ask him that question. You have already ruled and so I will go forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Krzic, you told us during your direct examination that -- let me just refer to the actual transcript. It's page 1481. Mr. Koumjian asked you this question: "Mr. Krzic, were you aware, in Banja Luka, in 1992, did you hear the sound of explosions at night?" And your answer was: "Yes, every night." Correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I think you said that some nights there were more than one explosion?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you actually mean that every night between April and December, 1992, there were explosions in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally speaking, yes. Whether or not there was a night without explosions, let me tell you, we would notice such nights immediately. These are details, but in my opinion, I think it was every night.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So if there were 275 nights between April and December, it's your testimony to this Trial Chamber that there were more than 275 explosions in Banja Luka during that time?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there were -- there was a large number.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: At page -- well, I'm not sure of the page. There was a page in the transcript, testimony in the transcript, and you may or may not recall it, you were asked by Mr. Koumjian about the confiscation of businesses and apartments when the bombing stopped, and your answer was, "Yes, however, the shelling, the bombings, did not stop altogether." The question I have is, there never was any shelling of Banja Luka, was there?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you say shelling, I assume that you mean firing of projectiles from cannons or mortars. As far as I know there was no shelling from the opposing side or from the army of BH so to say, but the lines were at about 50 kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Could the witness be given a copy of Prosecution Exhibit 461, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Krzic, the document that's been handed you is Prosecution Exhibit 461, and it has to do with a 22 June, 1992, meeting with General Talic, does it not?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And a number of people were present at that meeting, Mufti Halilovic, Dr. Duric, Dr. Sirbegovic, Medic, Professor Bajric, and you; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you were there representing the SDA and these people were representing various other Islamic Muslim organisations of one form or another?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the purpose of this meeting was to try to seek the help of General Talic regarding the safety of Muslims in the Banja Luka area; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only in Banja Luka but in the surrounding places too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And General Talic was in a position to have been aware, of course, of the political makeup of the Banja Luka area since he lived there, correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. Now, this document was prepared, I take it, after the meeting as a memorandum of what had occurred in the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And was it prepared by you or was it prepared by someone else?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was prepared in the presence of the participants, but I printed it on the machine.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And then, after having an opportunity to review it for its accuracy, all of these people from all these various organisations signed it, correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And it was important to all the people who were present at that meeting from the various Muslim organisations that this document be an accurate record of what had gone on in that meeting, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One would assume so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you record in this document that each of these persons signed that General Talic had advised that Muslims should contact the Crisis Staff of Banja Luka Municipal Assembly to request visits to collection centres and concentration camps and everything else connected with this, correct? Now I'm asking you isn't that what it says?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is what's contained in the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I now want to go into the pile of documents that you've been given that are marked as Defence exhibits and I think there is a copy that we had given to the Registrar for Mr. Krzic to refer to. And I'd ask that that be given to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Krzic, what I'll be doing as we go through these documents is basically asking you if you have seen the document before, referring you to language in the document and simply asking you if that language is true or not true, okay?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document is one that I see for the first time. The Glas, the newspaper Glas is familiar to me, of course, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment because I don't think we can go ahead like this. The witness has gone straight on to a document and I don't even know which document he's talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I understand. He misunderstood my instructions. I'm going to ask him -- I was getting ready to interrupt him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Krzic, the first document that you should see is DB2, It's marked as DB2. It's English. And DB2B is in B/C/S and it's an article from a newspaper, the headline being, "Krzic Provokes Chaos." You have that document in front of you, do you not?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the writer, apparently, is someone who is writing a letter to the editor of this newspaper and he's claiming that it's not true when you said, "We are asked to sign a declaration of our loyalty to the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. He's just suggesting that that's not a true statement on your part if, in fact, you ever made that statement. And tell me your reaction to that.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To give you a correct answer, I would have to -- I would have had to read this article previously. So to give you an answer in a few seconds, which concerns an article which I see for the first time now, for your sake and for the sake of the speed of this trial, I can make a few Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. comments but I can't make a proper comment. What I can say is that it seems to concern someone who is a very chauvinistic person and who wants to provoke chaos. It is not I who wants to provoke chaos. And you can see below that the same man gives such -- makes such statements. The purpose of which is to provoke chaos. That is my comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Go now to the next document which is DB3. This appears to be a statement given by a person named [redacted] Do you know [redacted]

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And [redacted] is a Muslim, is he not?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Koumjian?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry for not interrupting earlier, but I'm wondering if dealing with these documents, and I believe these are reports from the security service, and they concern basically statements or interrogations of individuals, it wouldn't be better to go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think that's a wise suggestion, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's fine with me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, we will now go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session now, Madam Registrar, no?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm sorry to have interrupted you like this, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But it just occurred to my mind and perhaps the witness can answer the question. The question is, in case you have lost track, Mr. Krzic, and I wouldn't blame you if you did, Mr. Ackerman read out to you another part from the New York Times report, particularly where it alleges that you said, after saying that Banja Luka is the last ghetto for Muslims and Croats in the region, you also said that, "If the purges start here, they won't be able to be stopped." And Mr. Ackerman's question is whether you said that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot remember that statement, but I do assert that using a metaphor, Banja Luka could have already then been described as a ghetto for non-Serbs and I stand by that. There are two statements here on the same page, but the question is, when I made that statement, whether it may have been a month previously or on the same day as the statement by Lord Owen. If it was on the same day that Lord Owen was in Banja Luka, then -- and not just I, but Mr. Hadzagic was with me. We made a statement about the crimes being committed throughout the region and specifically in Banja Luka. And there were quite sufficient elements there to make it clear that genocide had begun, not just eviction and ethnic cleansing, an expression that does not correspond to the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Krzic, can we return now to my question. My question was: You are quoted in that article as saying, "If the purges start here, they won't be able to be stopped." My question is: Did you say that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really -- I told you other things, worse things, but now the question is when what was said, at the time at which things were said, and I can't tell that time from this. My position was clear. I had that position. If they start deporting people, there will be no end to it. That's quite clear. If en masse killings commence, we won't be able to put an end to it. I don't see what is in dispute here. That's clear. The only thing that is in dispute or is contentious is the fact that you are contending my statement, and you haven't given the basic elements, the basic facts, when the statements were given, under what circumstances, because I'm referring to the press conference in the Bosna Hotel where there were -- I'm referring to the press conference in the Bosna Hotel where there were scores of foreign journalists, and where these words, not these words, not "if it begins" but the words "it has already begun" were used. If mass killing has already commenced, then ethnic cleansing is a secondary matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I hate to risk asking you a third time to answer my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you would be risking the Chamber stopping you now. I think he has given you an answer in a way which maybe you did not expect, but has given you an answer and I don't think you will get any further with the witness on this matter because he is drawing parameters around it, depending on what time are we talking about, which particular point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Could I get the usher's assistance with another document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want the witness to see the first page just to see the date of the publication and the order, and then I'm going to refer to the second page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Krzic, you see that what we are looking at here is an article from Newsday, written by Roy Gutman, September 25, 1992. You know Mr. Gutman, do you not?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you have meetings with Mr. Gutman?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You've actually had Mr. Gutman as a guest in your home, have you not?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not as a guest, a visitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And as an a visitor in your home, you've gotten to respect him and you believe that he is a respectable journalist, correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Could we look then at page 2 of this document? And look down toward the bottom, the yellow part down toward the bottom starting with, "Until now." "Until now, Banja Luka, the principal city in northern Bosnia, has been largely spared the terror tactics of ethnic cleansing, the process of emptying territory of unwanted ethnic groups." That's what Mr. Gutman wrote in September of 1992. Do you agree with him?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree. Ethnic cleansing started a lot earlier. I describe scenes of ethnic cleansing not in the way that you imagine them, but scenes involving many planes which were leaving Banja Luka. And now I will use a metaphor. They were leaving Banja Luka as if it were before the fall of Saigon, and I can bear witness to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Could I have those documents returned, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If we need to go into private session again, Mr. Ackerman, please tell me in good time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour. Your Honour, I'm sorry to be taking time but I'm skipping some material just in the interests of trying to finish. If you'll just give me a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I understood that from the way you were handling those papers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Would you look, Mr. Krzic, at Defence Exhibit DB22A?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And if you look at it, there is a B/C/S version. It's a copy of an article from a newspaper, and the first thing I'll ask you is have you seen this article previously?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, an article? Ah, on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I make a suggestion, just for the clarity of everyone when we are reading the transcripts months later, that we just indicate that, for example, this document is from Glas Srpska on the 9th of August, 1994, it will make it easier for us all to identify what was being talked about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I appreciate that Mr. Koumjian, and perhaps Mr. Ackerman takes the suggestion, which the Chamber makes its own.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we had agreed to something similar or along those lines already, before.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Have you seen the article before?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I can't remember, but I know that I received an oral report about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It makes a rather scurrilous allegation against you regarding an embezzlement of money in London, and I take it that your position is that's absolutely not true. And that's not the part I'm really interested in unless you want to tell me it is true. The part I'm interested in is the part of the article headed, "I Saved the People of Vecici." And you'll find it in the English version on page 3. And it purports to be quoting from you, quoting you as saying, if you'll look at the last couple of sentences, "Do not hold it against me that I am pointing this out but my humble self played a role there. The people of Vecici know this best and that is a story in itself, an epic tale." Did you say that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's really difficult to remember the words, whether I said this at some point or not. But that I saved Vecici, the people of Vecici, I would never be able to claim such a thing. Because when the people from Vecici are in question, my role finished with my visit and with my report to the International Red Cross on what was happening there. As well as on the report of the journalists who visited me then. This is when my role finishes in the matter of Vecici. So unless you consider this to be saving them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I suggest to you, Mr. Krzic, that throughout this period of 1992 and into 1993, that what you were doing was making exaggerations and false claims to media and to government organisations for the purpose of trying to draw attention to yourself and to aggrandise yourself and to draw attention of the West to Banja Luka and the situation there, and many of your claims were false, not true; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree with that. I'm under oath here and I have spoken about things that I know of. If there were any errors, I was convinced that it was important to say what I knew. It wasn't a time -- at that time scientific work was not in question. It wasn't possible to use references or to use libraries so I wouldn't agree with your conclusion. My intention was not to aggrandise my role because that entailed danger. But what I did was something that others members of the SDA did too, to a greater or lesser extent. They appeared in public. If you consider that to be a way of exaggerating one's role, if you consider that appearing at a press conference amounts to doing this, for example, in Hotel Bosna in the presence of -- well, we know very well who was present there, if you think this is a way of trying to improve one's image, then I'm very puzzled by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We have to go back into private session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We will go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are in public session now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: This document basically is lists of candidates from the various political parties in the municipal elections in 1990 for the municipality of Banja Luka, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time I have this document before me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The question is: It is a list of candidates --

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it is. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What I'd like you to do is look at page 3 where the list for the SDS begins, and it contains, I believe, 130 candidates.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You do not see on that list the name of Radoslav Brdjanin anywhere among that 130, do you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume it isn't there, because he wasn't a citizen of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So your contention that he would have been part of the Banja Luka municipality Crisis Staff would also not have been possible because he wasn't a citizen of Banja Luka, correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but the headquarters of the crisis -- of the regional Crisis Staff was also in Banja Luka, as far as I know. At least it had meetings there very often.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I was talking about the municipal Crisis Staff of Banja Luka, not the regional Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to you look at 32B. These are the B/C/S versions of the documents under 32A.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think I must say for the record that all of these documents, beginning with 31, are just rough draft translations that were done unofficially. I received these documents last Wednesday. I wanted to use them this week and so I asked that they be translated on an emergency basis, unofficially, and if the Court does not want me to use these unofficial translations, of course, I won't, but I need to disclose to you that that's what they are. They are not CLSS translations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Koumjian or Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: That's not a problem. I don't know if this would save any time, but if counsel's line of questioning is going to prove that Mr. Brdjanin was neither a member of the Municipal Assembly of Banja Luka nor the Crisis Staff for the Municipality of Banja Luka, that's not our contention. We are willing to stipulate that he was not a member of those.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I appreciate that. And that's not where I'm going, but it's not to have the stipulation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Krzic, you have contended that your representatives, the SDA representatives, walked out of the assembly of the municipality of Banja Luka early in 1992, correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from the assembly, which was considering -- which was discussing changes, amendments to the statute, and joining ZOBK, the Association of Municipalities. I would have to have a look at that again, but don't rely on what I'm saying. I can't remember exactly. It could have been the autonomous region, but I'll have a look and then I can tell you, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And following that, in meetings with Mr. Vance and Mr. Owen, you were urged to have your deputies return to the assembly, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Don't use the plural. Lord Owen made this suggestion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. What I'd like you to do is look through these documents. Can you identify these documents that are the documents in 32B? Can you tell the Trial Chamber what these documents are?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that these are confirmations of presence of deputies at various sessions of the municipal assembly. Several assemblies are in question here, several sessions of the assembly are in question, the 27th, the 24th, et cetera. These are just examples.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We don't have time to go through each and every entry, but would you agree with me that the people whose names appear here are, if not completely, at least primarily, non-Serb delegates to the assembly, either Muslims or Croats? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It's obviously -- these are obviously certificates that have been selected.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: They are participating in the assembly all the way from May through October of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that. It has to be compared with the sessions; and secondly, you should know that, as far as I can see, the names here, the names of the deputies, I can see names of deputies from the SDP and from the Reformist Party. Of course the SDA is here too. I can't remember which sessions they attended and which ones they did not. This information must be found in some other way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we now have copies of the documents that we didn't have earlier. They've been marked with exhibit numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Could I ask Mr. Ackerman for a copy? I gave all 12 copies to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You do have this one, don't you?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the interpreters have a copy as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We are trying to get them to you. We have enough for you, I think. We always think of the interpreters first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please, proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do we have a set of the documents for Mr. Krzic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Look, please, at Exhibit DB37A, and this is just --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Ackerman, the interpreters still do not have their copies.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Have the copies been -- okay, thank you. So I suppose you can proceed, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Krzic, we are looking at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 37A, you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- 37A, and this is a document dated 7 August 1992. It comes from the Banja Luka Citizens Council. What is that? What is the Banja Luka Citizens Council?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had a gathering, an informal one, of intellectuals who would meet occasionally, ever since 1990, or later, and who reviewed the situation purely from the standpoint of getting insight into the situation, and endeavouring to overcome difficulties. Later, some SDA members, I think, but I'm not 100 per cent sure, developed this new name known as the Citizens Council of Banja Luka, and that is what is referred to in this document. It is synonymous, if I can put it that way, yes, well -- by this name, several people could be covered. I would receive a document of this kind that was signed and it would be up to me to forward it and add any comments, if I had any to add. I did not write such documents, but I did receive them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: This organisation was a multi-ethnic organisation, then, made up of Bosniaks, Croats, Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can just tell you about my impressions. I really don't know who they were. I even think that it was a multi-ethnic group.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you weren't a member of that group, were you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: On page 1, in the second paragraph, the report indicates that, "On 6 August 1992, roundups were carried out at three points in Banja Luka because the Serbs, like the Croats and Muslims, will not respond to military call-ups." This means that Serbs were being arrested for failure to respond to military call-ups in the same way that Croats and Muslims were?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is common knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. If you look on page 3, bearing in mind this is a report of 7 August 1992, you'll see the language, "With the most recent" --

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's the last paragraph on page 3, "With the most recent massacre in the three villages mentioned, Banja Luka is next for ethnic cleansing with potentially dreadful consequences." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And, of course, the implication of that sentence is that as of 7 August, 1992, there had been no ethnic cleansing in Banja Luka, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of my earlier statements, I don't know whether there is a precise definition of ethnic cleansing. For me, ethnic cleansing is every form of abandoning one's native soil and property under coercion, whether it be of a psychological nature or direct physical threat. So that is my definition. I don't mind if other people have different definitions. And according to that definition, ethnic cleansing started much earlier. Whether each individual member you are mentioning now, the citizens council, each member of that council shared that same definition, I don't know, maybe that is up to experts to say. My definition is an empirical one. People left because of psychological pressure. It was sufficient to hear songs like, "We'll kill, we'll slaughter, wolves are killing and slaughtering. We will slaughter everything that is not Serb." That would be enough for people to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: This statement by the Banja Luka Citizens Council, August of 1992, that ethnic cleansing had not yet started in Banja Luka essentially, is consistent with a similar statement by Lord Owen that we just recently referred to in September of 1992, isn't it? Both of them saying basically the same thing?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to add something, Your Honours, that I think you should bear in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, are you answering my question?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you remember what the question was?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The question was, among other things, --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Krzic, answer the question. You don't have to explain back to Mr. Ackerman what the question was. If you've heard it you've heard it, and please proceed with your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to mention, Your Honours, that this document, if it was not attached among the documents that I had available to me in my book, I cannot say that the document was ever in my hands. So what I'm saying, it is quite possible for the intelligence service to have interfered and, as I see, it was very active. So if this document did pass through my hands, which means that I received it from people whose names I will give, if necessary, then I accept that I have seen this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So are you saying that it's possible that the intelligence service manufactured this document?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not claiming that. But a document that I did not send and that I did not have access to, it is very difficult for me to comment on. But, actually, I've already answered your question. I believe that ethnic cleansing started much earlier. And I've already given the explanation for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Look at Exhibit DB39, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know whether we are in or out of private session. We should be out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in public session at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you find this document?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: This is a letter dated 2 January 1993, sent apparently to Mr. Sacirbey at the BiH mission in the United Nations, correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's a report from a meeting held in the ICRC offices on 29 December, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: During that meeting, you say or somebody says, whoever wrote this, about halfway down the page, "It was pointed out that the ICRC should not issue statements about the problem of two Merhamets." What was the problem of two Merhamets?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Will you please tell me the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Page 1, halfway down.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What was the problem of two Merhamets?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the core of the problem was that a group within Merhamet, MDD of Merhamet, which is a charitable organisation at the level of Bosnia and Herzegovina, it is a member of an association of humanitarian organisations, I think, of the Red Cross and Red Crescent. In Banja Luka, there was a split in positions regarding the work of those organisations, but I think that the differences occurred because of the tense situation that prevailed there at the time. It wasn't a normal situation. And one half of Merhamet members got scared and agreed to register in the so-called Serb state, whereas the others did not. And they retained the original name, MDD Merhamet, and those who agreed to register called themselves MHD, that is, Muslim Humanitarian Organisation, voluntary organisation. That was the gist of it. We felt that this should not be over-emphasised, that both organisations should be allowed to engage in humanitarian activities, mainly feeding the population and providing the lowest level of medical care.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You've told us many times that Serbs were creating a climate of fear in an attempt to force non-Serbs to leave the Krajina region and ethnically cleanse the Krajina region, and that's your position, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a position contained in a series of documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you look at the second page of this document we are looking at now, under the heading, "Report 2," it says --

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- that at least 1700 Muslims left in the Sipovo municipality all of whom would already left had they been allowed. Who was keeping those people from leaving?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This report was obtained from a person that was in direct contact with Sipovo, because it had family members there, and I can only repeat what is written in the report, and I have quoted it literally. So I'd have to read the report and then tell you what it says, but you can do that yourself. But on condition that it is correctly translated, I agree with this report that I wrote.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You don't know, then, who was keeping them from leaving, whether it was Muslims that were holding them there or other people?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly the authorities at the time prevented it, because policies changed. They needed manpower in Sipovo in the woods there, and it depended on the degree of terror that existed, and it changed from one local community to another, from the structure of the authorities, and even it depended on individuals and their readiness to go to the extreme or not. So you would have to review several reports and see if the situation changed that later they were forced to leave. So, in my judgement here, they were kept there as labour, or even one might not exclude it, as a reserve force should a breakthrough be made by Croatian forces from Kljuc so they could be kept there as a shield. They may also be used for exchanges because I think this did occur, civilians were exchanged for Serb soldiers. So all these were possible options in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Look now at Defence Exhibit 40, would you please. This is an article of January 24th, probably 1993, from the newspaper Glas, and it has to do with a meeting that you had had with Mr. Radic, Mr. Predrag Radic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: One of the things you were trying to do was to get Mr. Radic to get the police involved in helping protect the Muslim people in Banja Luka, isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, I really have to put a question to you now. I won't put it in the original Bosnian version, but I need to read to see what this is about, because there were many similar meetings. I can give you an answer in principle, but you must tell me exactly which sentence you're referring to and I will confirm whether I said it or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. What I'm really referring to is something that Predrag Radic apparently told that newspaper with regard to demands that you had been making on him. I'll just ask you if you know whether or not this is true. Mr. Radic said that your demands that he do something --

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is true. Now I understand where you're heading so, please, continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What he had said to you was that the people you needed to talk to about control of the police were the head of the Ministry of the Interior, Mr. Alija Delimustafic, or Mr. Bajazid Jahic the chief of the Centre for Public Security Services, neither of whom Mr. Radic had any control over. That's what he told you, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, as far as I know, this is a statement for the press. This is not a conversation in his office. This is a statement for the press. So if Radic said something for the press, then that is probably so, for the Banja Luka Glas newspaper.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's true, isn't it, that the head of the Ministry of interior, which is the ministry that has authority over the police, was Alija Delimustafic, a Bosniak?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, my objection is it depends upon, obviously the answer, upon the date and this article is not dated. I have a very firm belief that this is January 1992. I don't know if counsel wants to stipulate to that it does mention General Vukovic, who was General Talic's predecessor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah. It would be January, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If that is the case, your objection is sustained for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In January, 1992, it's true s it not that Alija Delimustafic was Minister in Interior of Bosniak?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really have to say that I assume that was so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's true, is it not, that a Bosniak, Bajazid Jahic, was chief of the Centre for Public Security Services?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he was deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In the course of that article, down toward the end, last paragraph on page 3, --

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- Mr. Radic indicates that you failed to keep your word about something, and therefore he doesn't trust you any more. Was that the end of your relationship with Mr. Radic or did it take up again from there?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you know, that was not the end. There were meetings. Do I need to comment on his statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No, I don't think you do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have a great deal more material, but I've basically committed to you that I would finish at this time, and I think most of what the other material that I would cover is simply along the same line, cumulative perhaps, and so I think it would be appropriate that I conclude my cross-examination at this point. And I thank you for your patience. Thank you Mr. Krzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. Ackerman. Do you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, I do, about ten minutes. I don't know, do you want me to start it now or after the break? Whichever the Court would like me to proceed at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would rather prefer to have a response from the interpreters before I say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the interpreters would prefer a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Koumjian, we are going to have a short break. We will resume -- it's half past 12.00. We will resume at ten to 1.00, trying to make it a little bit shorter this time, and then you have your ten minutes. In the meantime, we will discuss to see whether we are going to put any questions. I personally do not have any questions to the witness. And then we can discuss the few remaining things that we have. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Just for the Court's information, I did plan to show a very short video of about two minutes and I have the transcript to be distributed. I can distribute that during the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: To the witness or after the witness has finished?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: To the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: To the witness, okay. Please have it prepared so that we can start with it and not waste time when we resume the sitting. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please, be seated. Mr. Ackerman, Ms. Korner, I understand that the documents saga has been solved.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have just been told that very kindly by Mr. Ackerman's colleague as we all thought it was a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Like everyone else around here, they went off to spend sometime in the Milosevic trial. They are back now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Koumjian, how do you want to proceed, with the video first or with questioning?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: A few questions and I'll finish with the video. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Krzic, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, there will be a short re-examination of you by the Prosecution. After that, there may be one or two questions from the Chamber and then I think you can pack your things and go back to your destination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Krzic, I'm referring, for counsel's benefit, to the document that was marked DB24, but do you recall you were asked about some statements made by Mr. Djuzel in a report or a statement to the State Security Service? And that report was dated the 2nd of September, 1994. Do you recall being questioned about that this morning?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was at the end, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Krzic, where Mr. Djuzel was on the 2nd of September, 1994?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you know if he was free?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't remember the exact date of his arrest, not the second time he was arrested. I was in Banja Luka when he was arrested the first time, but I would have to look. I would have to verify to see when he was arrested for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: The answer would be, you do not know whether he was in the custody of the State Security at the time he made that statement, correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say that until I have a look at the documents, but documents were shown to me when he was in prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Going on to DB30, you were asked about being charged with espionage, along with Mr. Djuzel, and an amnesty being passed. Is it correct that the amnesty was passed -- let me ask a question, excuse me. Was the amnesty passed before or after the Dayton Accords?
