utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was after the Dayton Accords.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: By the way, do you know if Mr. Djuzel was convicted of a crime by the authorities in Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The military court convicted him of a crime, for a series of crimes. I couldn't mention all of them, but one of them was that he was a member of a spy group.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you know what the possible punishment was for being a member of a spy group or for espionage at the time Mr. Djuzel made his statement on the 2nd of September, 1994? If you don't know, simply say you don't know.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know; the death penalty.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Going back to the first day of Mr. Ackerman's cross-examination of you, you were asked some questions about -- well, he read to you a statement that Mr. Karadzic made at a SDS deputies meeting concerning Mr. Brdjanin, and then asked you if that would change your view that Karadzic and Brdjanin were close together or Brdjanin would follow Karadzic, just to remind you of the context. And you indicated it did not change your view and you gave your reasons. Later, you added, "And Karadzic" -- you said you had forgot to mention, "Karadzic confirmed my views." Can you explain what you meant by that statement, that Karadzic later confirmed your views?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read it very quickly, but I think that Karadzic said that he was an extreme sort of person and that he was extremist in regard -- with regard to other nationalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Later in 1992, did Mr. Karadzic appoint Mr. Brdjanin to any positions, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not a single appointment in the so-called republic, the Republika Srpska, couldn't pass without the authorisation of Karadzic and I think that he was also appointed as president of the Crisis Staff of the autonomous region, and this was authorised by Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Later in 1992, was Mr. Brdjanin, to your knowledge, appointed to any position on the republic level?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a deputy of the republican assembly. Sorry, I didn't understand you. Do you mean later in 1993 or when?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: To your knowledge, in 1992, was Mr. Brdjanin appointed to any position in the government of the Republika Srpska, at the republic level, not at the regional level?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was a minister in the government, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: After that appointment, did you continue to see him or have knowledge of him being active in the Banja Luka area?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was very active in the media of all kinds. This is what was most accessible to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You were asked by Mr. Ackerman about a statement contained in one of the statements you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor wherein you said, regarding Mr. Brdjanin, he was the right person to organise ethnic cleansing camps and deportation. You were asked if you had any proof and you said that was your opinion, but you have certain facts behind it, nevertheless. My -- your exact answer is, "My personal opinion is based on certain facts, nevertheless." What facts did you base your opinion upon? The transcript that I have printed out from the LiveNote, that's page 73 of the testimony on day 11, that's February 7th, line 19.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I base my conclusions on the public appearances of Mr. Brdjanin, during which he was very explicit and stated that he was against coexistence, the coexistence of various peoples and in which the non-Serbs, especially the Bosniaks, in which he called them all sorts of names, derogatory names, and he threatened the non-Serbian population in his statements, and the Serbs who had moderate positions with regard to multi-ethnic coexistence and assistance were also threatened. This is what I base my conclusion on. And I also base it on the fact that he was a member or a high ranking official of such well-known organisations and institutions, such as the Crisis Staff or the government of the autonomous region of the Bosnian Krajina and beyond. Furthermore, I base this position on numerous testimonies given by Banja Luka people of Banja Luka who had been expelled. I collected these -- I listened to such statements throughout this various countries in Scandinavia and recently in Sarajevo, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: In 1993, when you went to Zagreb, were you able in Zagreb to listen or watch any media from Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not from Banja Luka, because they weren't made in public, but individuals would bring certain extracts from Glas. I received those.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Testimony about 1993, that's outside the scope of the indictment, things that Mr. Brdjanin might have said in 1993, if that's where this is going. I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, what do you have to say to that, Mr. Koumjian?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to move on to the video which does come from a statement made in 1993, but the accused's intent is very much at issue in this case and his state of mind. It also goes to statements by the witness and the implied attacks upon the credibility of the witness as far as his reports of statements he heard Mr. Brdjanin make in 1993 and 1993, which he testified to on direct and cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I'll also object to the playing of a video from 1993 because that's also irrelevant to the charges in the indictment. Mr. Brdjanin is not charged with anything during 1993 and it should not be permitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Bad news, Mr. Ackerman. Your objection is dismissed. The reason is very simple, that we cannot a priori decide that what Mr. Brdjanin may have said in 1993, or even later, will not or could not possibly throw a light on what may have happened in 1992 or what he may have been involved in, in 1992. So we will first hear what evidence is brought forward in regard and then, obviously, if it is definitely material which is irrelevant, it will be struck off from the memory of the Trial Chamber, if not from the records any way. Yes, Mr. Koumjian, please do remember also, when we come to this admissibility of evidence business, that this is a Trial Chamber made up of professional judges and not lay jurors. So we are not easily impressed with this or that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour I'm ready to play the video. My only question is I presume that this should receive a number. The video is with the audio-visual people, but perhaps it should receive the next Prosecution number in order for this particular segment of the video.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be P463.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And perhaps the English translation would be -- perhaps the video would be 463A, the English translation 463B and the B/C/S transcript, 463C? Would that be a good idea? No?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I mean, go 463A for the English, 463B for the Serbian and C for the -- because everything -- so far A and B has been A English, B Serb Croat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you are right, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: That sounds like a great idea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can we proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, may the video be played now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Krzic, I'd ask you to direct your attention to the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So far, we have a still picture.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] Brothers and sisters, dear citizens of Krajina and all other patriots attending this gathering. We must not be tricked into believing we are voting for peace or war. We are voting for the betrayal or the salvation of Republika Srpska. The leftists who are offering us again to live together must know that the obligation of the Serbs for the next 100 years is to wipe the shoes of this non-Christian scum who ... this country of ours. Moreover, it is not true that we do not know where our borders are. Our borders are from Benkovac from Trebinje. Our borders are from the Hungarian border all the way to Sokolac, with Belgrade, I hope, as its capital. We must tell the world that no one has the right to proclaim those we defeated the victors because this is the homeland of Tsar Dusan, Tsar Lazar, Karadjordje, and the Serbian heroes of today. I am asking as many of you as possible, to go to the referendum. And let me warn you, this referendum is an offer to us to hand over 20 settlements, including 13 towns. It is an offer to us to go back to Alija and Tudjman and to live with them. And I propose we put up barbed wire and say that never again will our enemies swagger on Krajina Square and attack us for the fifth or fourth time in this century. The worst thing is that it is now occurred to some of them that we should not have waged this war in the first place. As if it was us who imposed this war. Now it has dawned on some of them that the NATO alliance is dangerous. Do these gentlemen know that the lives of all of us who are married and who have children are of much less value than the lives of the young men lying in their graves? In their names, may I say that everyone who betrays the Republika Srpska and the interests of the Serbian people be damned. Cheers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Krzic, in the video you just saw -- first of all, do you recognise the speaker in that video?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Who was the speaker in the video?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you recognise the location where Mr. Brdjanin was speaking?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't pay much attention to that, but I think it is in the centre of town, the terrace below the high-riser in the centre of town, the skyscraper.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: In Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Banja Luka, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Had you seen this video before, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you understand Mr. Brdjanin to say, and I'm now referring to page 4, the ERN number 01107360 in the English translation, the 7th line down, the last two words of that line, "And I propose we put up barbed wire, say that never again will our enemies swagger on Krajina square and attack us for the fourth or fifth time in this century." Can you tell me as a person from Banja Luka who lived there in 1992, how did you understand these words, that I propose we put up barbed wire? And saying that [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And say that never again will our enemies swagger on Krajina square.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand that in two ways. The formation of concentration camps and, secondly, drastic ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Could I ask you now to refer to the B/C/S transcript, page 3, and that would be -- do you have that in front of you, sir?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And I'm particularly going to direct your attention, I'm going to mark in red the fifth line down, that line appears on the English translation, if I'm not correct, refers to the sentence in the English translation of saying, this is on page -- the first page of the English translation, ERN number 01107359 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Koumjian, I don't think we have these two documents that you are mentioning. Which ones? Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And perhaps, Mr. Krzic, you can find in B/C/S the sentence I'm going to read in English. The sentence in English is, "The leftists were offering us again to live together, must know that the obligation of the Serbs for the next 100 years is to wipe the shoes of this non-Christian scum who," a word was not translated, "This country of ours."

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: First of all, can you tell me, as a person who has lived in Banja Luka during that time period, how did you understand this sentence, referring to leftists who are offering us again to live together?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The leftists is a definition linked to the former communist parties, but in those days it could be linked to all democratic political or other forces. And in that context, to me, this means that for him, leftists are all humanists, all real democrats, and normal people, if I can put it that way. As for the second part of this sentence, it is horrifying because, in my opinion, it says that non-Serbs will be exposed to the worst possible kind of terror, a metaphor is used, by saying that non-Serbs are dirty beings, that every Serb has the right to beat, as he can hit a dirty dog in the street, that his sole responsibility is to clean his shoes that have been dirtied in the process. So I understand that as being the task of each Serb to take part in the extermination of entire peoples.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I don't have any further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Koumjian. Mr. Krzic, the Trial Chamber has a few questions to put to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: My question was partly answered in re-examination, but any way, Mr. Krzic, could you tell me the time, I mean year and month, of the trial in absentia for espionage, if you remember. I think you remember.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was the end of 1994. Please don't ask me to be too precise. But any way, it was the end of 1994. Yes. That was when the proceedings were conducted. But the arrest, I'm afraid at this moment, I can't recollect. I would have to look it up in my notes, of course. I took great care about these things but just now I can't remember the birthdays of my children, but I do know the year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Thank you. That's okay. Thank you. That's enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: My first series of questions concern to transcript pages from 1615 to 1621. On Wednesday of last week, in summary, you testified that Bosnian Muslims were able to declare as Muslims under the 1974 constitution, but ethnic name based on religion affiliation is not relevant. The term Bosniak is traditionally accepted term even from Austro-Hungarian times. At the time of 1974 constitution, the Bosniaks were neither consulted through referendum, nor, adequately represented through deputies; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Muslims were not consulted as to whether they wanted the name Muslim or some other name, that is true. Secondly, the Muslims came to be called Muslims and were recognised as such much earlier. I said in Mrkonjic, during the session of Zavno-BiH, which was a de facto and de jure recognition of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: According to your understanding, not only you but almost all Muslims in Bosnia-Herzegovina have had their aspiration to be called Bosniaks from long before?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that in our tradition and in our history, earlier history, before Yugoslavia was formed, Muslims were treated as Bosniaks. Of course, it is hard to convey any precise feelings of a broad spectrum because there were no inquiries conducted into this matter so that I can only convey my personal opinion. I must admit that we came used to be calling Muslims and we preferred that name, though obviously it was linked exclusively to our religion. But we preferred to be called that than having to decide -- opt to be either Serbs or Croats. So that I am not able to answer your question with certainty except by saying what my own personal opinion is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: But such an aspiration of Muslims were well known or not well known amongst Serbs and Croats?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were known. There were so many intellectuals at the state Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. level from Bosnia-Herzegovina, even before that elucidated our ethnic ethnological and other affiliations through various studies and research work. And there are well-known papers by some prominent intellectuals of Bosnia-Herzegovina along those lines. So I would prefer to refer to them than to my personal opinion because their studies were based on exact information and data.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: In your first statement, page 4, you said, "We Bosniaks had the first possibility to express our nationality for 70 years." As to the term "Bosniaks," you expected some negative reaction from Serbs or Croats?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In those days, that is after the democratic changes, as we called them, we did not expect any opposition among the people to such a name, because, after all, that name was well known. However, one could expect certain political circles, and I'm still talking about the period prior to the elections, that is, political circles in communist Yugoslavia might try to deny this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: In your statement dated 23rd August, 1995, that is your first statement, on page 5, at almost the end of the third paragraph of English version, you said, "I attended the November, 1991, SDA congress in Sarajevo, where I gave a speech which was well-received. The people in Sarajevo did not really believe me when I warned them of what could happen." Then my first question is: What was the gist of your speech at that occasion? Can you remember the content of your speech at that time?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can remember in broad lines, of course. I wanted to warn that in Banja Luka a wave of greater Serbian nationalism had started to spread, which was still rather mild but which could be felt, particularly in the official institutions and at the university, and that was also one of the reasons why my daughter had to go to Sarajevo to study, where I had to rent a room for her and pay for it, which meant additional expenses, simply to avoid the psychological pressure that already existed at the university in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: In your statement dated February 15th, 2001, that is your third statement, on page 2 of the English version, you mentioned you had a code name. Approximately when you thought about using a code name?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wrote in my book the exact date when I started to use it, and, Your Honour, it's really difficult for me to remember the date without looking it up in the book, but I can do that. I gave myself this code name in the naive belief that this might save me should I be taken to court. However, in real terms, that was extremely naive on my part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: I would like to know exactly when you began to use your code name.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, I'd really have to look that up in the book. I think it was in 1993, but I'd really have to look it up. The exact date is given in my book, and I stand by that. The Prosecutor, I think, can provide that date subsequently, and I abide by what I said in the book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: Not in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. I think it was much later. I really can't remember, because it wasn't a decision taken. It was an idea that I had, and it is actually the name of the wife of my associate in the United States of America who received messages, Hamdija Todorovac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krzic. I think that brings to an end your evidence. Yes, Mr. Koumjian?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I remember the Court's admonition quite a while ago, last week, about the exhibits and I should be sure to move those into evidence while he's still here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: So I at this time move into evidence the exhibits that were shown to him and that would be up to Exhibit 463 that was shown today.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would do the same with the Defence exhibits that were presented. I don't know the full range of numbers. I can provide that, but I think the recommendation already has them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you referring, because actually we were discussing that during the break, and we were coming back to you on this, are you intending to exhibit even those documents which you did not put questions to Mr. Krzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I would like to, because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On what basis?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If I'd had time I would have asked him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the present moment you might require them later on for some other witness. But at the present moment, we can only look at these documents as documents, some of them, that have not been made use of.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's fine. The Prosecution has a lot of documents that are in the record that have not been made use of either, that have already been admitted. So I don't see any reason why mine can't be admitted under the same circumstances. And if I refer to them later, and you find they have some weight, you can give them weight; if I don't, whatever. You're professional judges. You can do whatever you want with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you live with that, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think we probably can. All I was concerned about is I don't think either of us have checked what the other documents were. Could we perhaps -- I take Mr. Ackerman's point that we are going to move into evidence perhaps on Monday a lot of documents. Why do I say move into evidence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We could live with that because later on when we start sifting the wheat from the chaff we are going to pay attention as to what was made use of and what was not made use of, and we are certainly not the type of judges that we will just select those documents that were not made use of and come back to you to enlighten us further.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I think we can move ahead along those lines, have them admitted and then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we were trying to find a way of trying to make life easier for you and for us, but more or less we are in agreement that it is perhaps more practical to go ahead for the moment as has been suggested; in other words, admit all these documents as exhibits, and we may come back to this system later on if need be. But for the time being we can go ahead like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is one matter. Despite our best efforts, as Your Honour will hear when we go through the whole Banja Luka documents, we have managed to mark two exhibits twice again; in other words, we pre-marked the Banja Luka documents. But two of them, Mr. Krzic referred to and they were given a different number. And I think the simplest thing, because it's on the index, if Your Honour goes to -- does Your Honour have a copy of the index?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I had it --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I deal -- Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Why don't you do it ... [Microphone not activated] ... And then report it back to.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I was suggesting that you do this in an informal way and then refer the agreement or whatever it is to Madam Registrar who will just regulate the numbering of the documents for us in due course. I mean we are not going to -- we are not concentrating now on the different numbers. That will -- we will come to that at a later stage if and when we come to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. All I was going to suggest was that you may want to mark your schedules accordingly. But I have a feeling we do not have any time today to deal with the documents, so perhaps I can deal with it on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Okay. In the meantime, you are exhibiting --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think, Your Honours, we are exhibiting the documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly, let's finish that first.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I think we gave Your Honours the numbers, and I think Your Honours agreed you would admit them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the same applies to you, Mr. Ackerman. I assume that you are keeping or that the Registry is keeping the same DB sequence of numbers that is shown on the documents, no?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I believe that's correct, that's what we are trying to do. And I just want to make sure that we are not going to remove a document from evidence because it has a duplicate somewhere else in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, no, definitely not, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It has been referred to by a number in the transcript and it has to stay there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's not what the Trial Chamber understood. In any case, just to make things clear to you, the admission of these documents as exhibits does not mean anything beyond the fact that they are being admitted as exhibits for the time being. We could revisit some of these documents and send them back to you later on, if we think they are not relevant and/or have no probative value or, on the face of them, they are definitely unacceptable as exhibits because of one reason or another.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I think I understand what Your Honour means. All I don't want because I've been watching it happen in another court is the confusion of documents marked exhibit and then with a stroke ID and nobody seems to know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, no. In real fact I again stress the point, Ms. Korner, that we are dealing with professional judges, and I mean, having this document in the records or not having it, and not look at it or ignore it, because of its content, or not having it at all, doesn't really make much difference. I mean, at the end of the day, our job is to give to each document the attention that it deserves.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think Your Honour will find, as with all these types of cases, that both Defence and Prosecution by the end of the day will have reduced the number of documents that we are going to ask to you look at in full.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Krzic is still here, but I assume because of the next case and because I know Your Honour's colleagues are in another trial this afternoon, we will be rising at a quarter to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will be rising in two minutes' time, and I'm afraid, despite all my -- Mr. Krzic, I think I ought, on behalf of the Trial Chamber, to thank you again for your patience, for your good manners and for all the information that you were kind enough to give to this Trial Chamber. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too, Your Honours. It was a honour to be a witness here before you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, then, before Your Honours rise -- I'll just wait while Mr. Krzic leaves the court. Your Honours, it's just about the timetable next week. We are not sitting tomorrow because I think it's court maintenance or something equally exciting, and next week is only a four-day week, again because of the holiday. Your Honours, what I suggest is on Monday morning, before we call evidence, we deal with the various outstanding administrative matters. I'll have Mr. Inayat here in case it's necessary. We have only for next week two witnesses. Does Your Honour have the list?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have the list. [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I was just -- yeah, I have a list. I suppose the next one is 7.87.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It is. And that, Your Honour, I think may assist Judge Janu. He's one of the people who was actually arrested so he will be able to give chapter and verse about all this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We were handed the transcript of his statement last week, at some point last week. I've gone through it. It's relatively two short statements.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't anticipate this witness to last more than a day and a half.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We've given him -- we thought he probably wouldn't last more than the Monday itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But obviously that's why I'm asking. The next witness, number 5 on the list, 7.168, by our estimation, is a more lengthy one and he's going to deal with a number of documents. I don't know whether either of my learned friends can assist as to whether he will in fact take the next three -- he will certainly be the whole of Tuesday in chief. I don't know whether either Mr. Ackerman or Madam Fauveau are able to assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know. Are you in a position to enlighten us on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think Ms. Korner is correct. We will need more than two witnesses next week. I think that will take up the whole four days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If we take an hour Monday morning to thrash the procedural matters that we have pending, maybe even more, I don't know. That leaves us Monday, Tuesday. Yeah, I think it would be safer to stick to two witnesses and then we'll see as we go along.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm grateful, because in fact it would have caused us some problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This witness in particular, the statements have just been handed down to us an hour ago, and I see that half is in B/C/S and half is in English. But they will be read by us in the course of the weekend, during the weekend, and more or less we would be in a better position to make an assessment. But I take your word that more or less we would be safe if we base our schedule or our agenda for next week on two witnesses. I think that should be a fair assessment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, just very quickly, there is one matter. I don't know whether Your Honours can deal with it. It's simply because it involves contacting the witness. Your Honours gave leave for one witness with some amendments to his statement that -- to be put in through Rule 92. There was discussion at the Status Conference which was never resolved, the informal conference, which was never resolved, really, about how they are going to be treated if they want protective measures. This gentleman has actually requested that his name not be revealed to the public, and we'd have to put in a motion obviously to deal with that. But if -- can we just as a general principle, unless there is any objection, can we take it that if protective measures are requested, then the statement itself, once tendered into evidence, would remain under seal until information which might reveal his identity had been redacted from it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What do you say to that, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no problem with that at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Ms. Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it seems quite evident to me. It's no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In fact, I think we can -- in the notes that I have, it says, "The Trial Chamber needs to agree on a system for dealing with this. It may be that when the Prosecution submits a statement, it can make a request for protective measures, of course as is necessary. Any approved protective measures could then be put in place prior to the statement being marked as an exhibit." I think we can move along those lines, as you have suggested. I see no danger. Rather it's almost an over-precaution. So I would go along with that without any hesitation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There being so objections or reservations on the part of the Defence. So I think we can end our labours for the week. Mr. Brdjanin and General Talic, we are not having a sitting tomorrow because maybe you've been informed already, it's a special day which the Tribunal here dedicates to some maintenance work, and so we will not be able to make use of the courtrooms. We will meet again, reconvene on Monday, at 9.00 in the morning. I'm not quite sure whether it's still in this courtroom. I think it is in Courtroom III. So have a nice weekend, and see you all on Monday. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: be reconvened on Monday, the 18th day of January, 2002, at 9.00 a.m.
